title: Database indexes
description: What an index buys, what it costs, and how to tell whether a query is using one.

questions.text: What does an index mainly speed up?

options.text: Reads that filter or sort on the indexed columns

questions.explanation: An index is an ordered structure the database can search instead of scanning the whole table.

questions.text: Adding more B-tree indexes to a table generally makes its inserts, updates and deletes slower.
questions.explanation: A write usually has to update each index that covers the changed row, so more indexes mean more work per write, and each index also takes space. The cost is real even though a few writes (for example a row that falls outside a partial index) skip some indexes.

questions.text: A composite index on (last_name, first_name) can efficiently serve which query?
questions.explanation: A composite index is ordered by its first column, then the second. A query must use a leftmost prefix of the columns to benefit.

questions.text: Which columns usually deserve an index? Select all that apply.

options.text: A foreign key used in frequent joins
A column in the WHERE clause of a hot query
A boolean column with a 50/50 split, filtered alone on a huge table

questions.explanation: Index what queries actually filter and join on. Low-selectivity columns rarely help on their own, and indexing everything slows writes.

questions.text: EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan on a large table even though an index exists. What is a likely cause?

options.text: The query wraps the indexed column in a function, so the index cannot be used

questions.explanation: WHERE lower(email) = ... cannot use a plain index on email. Rewrite the predicate or create an index on the expression. Two other usual suspects are a filter that matches a large share of the rows, where a sequential scan really is cheaper, and stale statistics.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL, orders.customer_id is declared as a FOREIGN KEY to customers(id), and you often fetch all orders for one customer. What do you need to do about indexing orders.customer_id?

options.text: Nothing, because PostgreSQL creates an index for every foreign key automatically
Create the index yourself, because PostgreSQL indexes primary keys and unique constraints automatically but not the referencing side of a foreign key
Nothing, because the index on customers(id) already speeds up lookups on orders.customer_id
Nothing, because foreign keys are only indexed when ON DELETE CASCADE is set

questions.explanation: The primary key on customers(id) is indexed, but orders.customer_id is a separate column in a separate table, and PostgreSQL does not index it for you. Without your own index, finding one customer's orders (and checking the foreign key when a customer is deleted) scans the whole orders table.

questions.text: Which single index serves this query best? SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 17 AND created_at >= '2026-01-01' ORDER BY created_at
questions.explanation: Put the equality column first and the range or sort column second. The index then jumps straight to customer 17 and reads that customer's rows already sorted by created_at from the start date. With (created_at, customer_id) the database has to walk every entry since the start date, for all customers, and check customer_id as it goes. An index on customer_id alone finds the right rows but leaves the date filter and the sort to extra work.
